name: Lexus LFA
hook: Toyota began as a loom company, and to build the LFA it went back to weaving — this time in carbon fibre.
story: Toyota did not begin with cars. It began with looms. Sakichi Toyoda built his first weaving machine in 1890, and in 1906 he invented a circular loom: the shuttle travelled round and round instead of back and forth, quietly and without stopping. Hold on to that. Now jump a hundred years. The LFA had been in development for five years, it was made of aluminium, and it was too heavy. Chief engineer Haruhiko Tanahashi had run out of ideas. Then the R&D boss, Kazuo Okamoto, tapped him on the shoulder. Get over it, he said. Go with carbon fibre, and make it here rather than buy it in. So they started the car over, and built a machine to weave the material: a circular loom, because a round weave comes off already shaped like a part. It wove the roof, the floor, the pillars, even the steering wheel. Two-thirds of the finished car is carbon. A loom company had gone round in a circle.
description: The LFA is a two-seat supercar built by Lexus at the Motomachi plant in Aichi, Japan. Its 4.8-litre V10 was co-developed with Yamaha and climbs from idle to 9,000 rpm in about 0.6 seconds — too quick, Lexus said, for the needle of an analogue rev counter, so the driver gets a screen instead. About 65 per cent of the body is carbon fibre, woven in-house. Five hundred cars were built between December 2010 and December 2012, at roughly one a day.
